Cabinet approves draft Armed Police Battalions Act, 2026
item.description:
By UNB

The cabinet on Monday approved the draft of Armed Police Battalions Act, 2026, with a view to modernising and making the force more people-friendly by abolishing the existing ordinance.

The approval came from the cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman at the Secretariat.

According to the proposed law, the Armed Police Battalion will be entrusted with responsibilities, including maintaining public security, providing security to VIPs and government-declared important installations, and taking action against those involved in terrorism, drug trafficking, human trafficking, rape and crimes against humanity.

The battalion, which is part of the police force, will also assist other law enforcement agencies in maintaining law and order.

The draft law also proposes empowering the members of the battalion to investigate criminal offences and conduct related proceedings, subject to compliance with the Code of Criminal Procedure and other laws.

It further proposes provisions for the establishment of special courts and summary courts and lays down procedures for conducting trials.

Under the proposed law, the Armed Police Battalion will operate under the control and supervision of an additional inspector general of police.

The draft law was prepared in Bangla, making the existing legal framework more up-to-date and the Armed Police Battalion more people-oriented.

The draft was uploaded on the website of the Ministry of Home Affairs to seek public opinion.

The proposed law seeks to repeal the Armed Police Battalions Ordinance, 1979, but retains the validity of actions taken under the existing ordinance.

The draft law was given final approval by the Cabinet subject to vetting by the Legislative and Parliamentary Affairs Division.

item.title: Nine years on, Rohingya still stranded as Bangladesh’s diplomatic strategy comes under scrutiny
item.description:
By bdnews24.com

Bangladesh must pursue constitutional reforms while keeping the original Constitution of 1972 as the foundation, Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman has said.

Part A of Article 6 of the July Charter repeatedly says these measures have to be carried out through constitutional amendments, he explained.

“That means I have accepted the 1972 Constitution as the basis. Whatever I do, I have to move forward with the 1972 Constitution before me. That is one part of my July Charter.”

Asaduzzaman was speaking as chief guest at a dialogue titled “Post-election Bangladesh: Political Promises and Reality” at the CIRDAP auditorium in Dhaka on Monday.

The Centre for Governance Studies (CGS) organised the event with representatives of the government and political parties, lawyers, journalists, human rights activists and members of civil society.

CGS President Zillur Rahman moderated the discussion.

The law minister said those who had argued for discarding the 1972 Constitution altogether would have offered a simpler route.

“If we had done what those who said the 1972 Constitution should be thrown away wanted, I could have gone down a straight line,” he said.

“But as long as the 1972 Constitution remains, I have to amend that Constitution. In going through the amendment process, I have to keep before me the points of the July Charter that we signed for reform.”

July Charter Order Questioned

Asaduzzaman also questioned the “July Charter Implementation Order” issued during the interim administration, saying it was inconsistent with the Constitution.

Explaining why an “order” had been issued rather than an ordinance, he said: “If this amounts to something equivalent to amending the Constitution, then it conflicts with the Constitution.

“An ordinance cannot be issued if it is equivalent to a constitutional amendment. That is why they did not go for an ordinance and instead issued an order.”

He then questioned the legal status of that order.

“What is the legal status of this order? Under the Third Schedule of the Constitution, the power to issue such orders ceased from the day the Constitution came into operation in 1972.

“Some laws were made through presidential orders in 1972, and those have the status of law. But it was also made clear that after the Constitution came into force, the president would no longer have the power to issue such orders.”

Asaduzzaman said laws must be passed by parliament, while ordinances can be issued when parliament is not in session.

He argued that by issuing the July Charter implementation order, the interim government had left behind a “path to division”.

‘You Have the Right to Hold Programmes’

The law minister later responded to questions raised by political leaders who had spoken earlier in the discussion.

Didarul Alam Bhuiyan, joint general secretary of Rashtra Sanskar Andolan, said his party had sought permission to hold a rally at the Central Shaheed Minar last Saturday but was denied permission because a case had been filed against one of its members.

The law minister said there was no law that could justify such a restriction unless the party itself was banned.

“There is no such law as long as your political party is not regarded as a banned political entity,” he said.

“Since your party is not banned, you can organise programmes and criticise the government there. You certainly did not enter politics to sing the government’s praises.

“You have that right, and it is the government’s responsibility to ensure that right. I hope we will address these issues.”

Constitution Reform Committee

NCP Joint Convenor Monira Sharmin raised the issue of the parliamentary committee on constitutional reform.

The law minister said the plan had been to form a 17-strong committee during the first session of parliament, with seven members from the BNP, five from the opposition alliance, and five from other political parties.

“We asked the opposition to give us five names, but they said they would provide them in the next session,” he said.

“We held repeated meetings but did not receive the names. We have now formed a 12-member committee.

“I hope that if they submit the names, we can move forward with constitutional amendments along the path of reform. We will try to incorporate any of your proposals if they are reasonable.”

Freedom of Expression, Extrajudicial Killings

Law Minister Asaduzzaman also addressed freedom of expression and extrajudicial killings.

“We are trying to move away from that culture,” he said.

“We have turned around and are trying to reach the right destination. Our pace may be slow, but look at the statistics and see what the situation with extrajudicial killings has been over the past six months.”

He also spoke about the Enforced Disappearance Prevention and Redress Act enacted during the interim government.

“I was the attorney general at the time,” he said. “The attorney general is never involved in vetting legislation.”

He said the law provided for trials over enforced disappearances both at the International Crimes Tribunal and in ordinary courts, but did not clearly specify which cases should go before which jurisdiction.

It also provided for a maximum punishment without setting a minimum sentence, he said. “The law was placed before parliament to correct these anomalies.”

Asaduzzaman said the government was trying to build a system of accountability.

“We are putting it into practice and will see how successful we can be. If it does not work, we are open to amendments.

“A law is not the Quran or the Bible that cannot be changed.”

Law Minister’s Interim Role Criticised

Gono Forum President Subrata Chowdhury challenged Asaduzzaman over his criticism of the former interim government.

“We now criticise the interim government so much. But he, the current law minister, was one of its strongest supporters,” Subrata said.

“The interim government could hardly move forward without his advice, and it trusted him.

“After doing all these things on behalf of the interim government, he has now joined this government and says he does not have that much power. We saw then how much power you had.”

Jatiya Party Secretary General Shameem Haider Patwary said many figures associated with the “spirit of July” had gradually disappeared from the political scene.

“We have gradually seen many people who embodied the spirit of July disappear completely. Now the spirit of July itself is also disappearing,” he said.

He argued that judicial reform had been the most urgent element of the broader reform agenda.

Bangladesh JaSaD Presidium Member Mushtuq Husain said his party had not signed the July Charter and had opposed the referendum.

“A referendum should take place after constitutional amendments,” he said. “There was language there that openly sought to discard the 1972 Constitution.”

He also strongly criticised Ali Riaz, who headed the Constitution Reform Commission.

Questions Over Foreign Policy

Sohrab Hasan, editor of the news outlet Charcha, raised questions about the government’s current foreign policy.

“The ruling party is silent about the US trade agreement, and so is the opposition,” he said. “We do not know where the government is heading in foreign policy.

“When war was imposed on Iran, our foreign ministry issued a statement as though Iran itself was responsible for the war.”

Prime Minister’s Political Advisor Zahir Uddin Swapon blamed the current energy problems on what he described as the previous government’s “political legacy”.

He argued that the crisis could have been avoided if the previous government had focused on extracting domestic energy resources such as gas instead of pursuing an import-dependent policy.

item.description:
চলতি অর্থবছরের প্রথম মাস জুলাইয়ে উন্নয়ন প্রকল্পে বরাদ্দের কোনো টাকাই খরচ করতে পারেনি সরকারের ১০টি মন্ত্রণালয় বা বিভাগ। পুরো বছরে এসব মন্ত্রণালয় ও বিভাগের প্রকল্পের অনুকূলে শত শত কোটি টাকা বরাদ্দ থাকলেও প্রথম মাসে টাকা খরচের খাতা শূন্য। ফলে প্রথম মাস শেষে সার্বিকভাবে বার্ষিক উন্নয়ন কর্মসূচির (এডিপি) ১ শতাংশ বাস্তবায়নও হয়নি।

আজ সোমবার পরিকল্পনা মন্ত্রণালয়ের বাস্তবায়ন পরিবীক্ষণ ও মূল্যায়ন বিভাগ (আইএমইডি) এডিপি বাস্তবায়নের হালনাগাদ চিত্র প্রকাশ করেছে।

প্রতিবেদনে বলা হয়, জুলাই শেষে সরকারের উন্নয়ন বরাদ্দের বিপরীতে ব্যয় হয়েছে মাত্র ২ হাজার ১২১ কোটি টাকা। চলতি অর্থবছরে এডিপিতে বরাদ্দ রাখা হয়েছে ৩ লাখ ৮ হাজার কোটি টাকা। সে হিসাবে টাকা খরচ হয়েছে মাত্র শূন্য দশমিক ৬৯ শতাংশ। শতাংশের হিসাবে যা গত অর্থবছরের সমান। এর আগের ২০২৪-২৫ ও ২০২৩-২৪ অর্থবছরের প্রথম মাসে অবশ্য ১ শতাংশের বেশি ব্যয় হয়েছিল।

সম্প্রতি সরকার অর্থবছরের সময়কাল বদলানোর সিদ্ধান্ত নিয়েছে। জুলাই–জুন সময়ের পরিবর্তে এপ্রিল–মার্চ সময় নির্ধারণ করা হয়েছে। ২০২৮–২৯ অর্থবছর থেকে নতুন সময়কাল ধরেই সবকিছু হবে। অর্থবছরের সময়কাল পরিবর্তনের অন্যতম কারণ হলো অর্থবছরের শুরুতে বর্ষাকাল হওয়ায় প্রকল্পের কাজ ঠিকমতো হয় না। বৃষ্টির কারণে অর্থবছরের শুরুতে উন্নয়ন প্রকল্পের টাকা খরচ করা সম্ভব হয় না। তাই উন্নয়ন প্রকল্পের টাকা যাতে আরও কার্যকরভাবে খরচ করা যায়, সে জন্য অর্থবছরের সময়কাল পরিবর্তন করার সিদ্ধান্ত হয়।

খরচ ‘শূন্য’ মন্ত্রণালয় ও বিভাগ কোনগুলো

জুলাই মাসে উন্নয়ন বরাদ্দ থেকে হিসাবে খাতা খুলতে না পারা অন্য মন্ত্রণালয়ের বা বিভাগগুলো হলো– শিল্প; বাণিজ্য; ধর্ম; পররাষ্ট্র; বেসামরিক বিমান পরিবহন ও পর্যটন; পাবর্ত্য চট্টগ্রামবিষয়ক মন্ত্রণালয়; স্বাস্থ্যসেবা বিভাগ; স্বাস্থ্য শিক্ষা ও পরিবার কল্যাণ বিভাগ; সেতু বিভাগ; অভ্যন্তরীণ সম্পদ বিভাগ। এসব মন্ত্রণালয় ও বিভাগ তাদের প্রকল্পের জন্য বরাদ্দ করা অর্থ খরচ করতে পারেনি।

বেশি ব্যয় করেছে কারা

বরাদ্দের বিপরীতে সবচেয়ে বেশি খরচ করেছে বাংলাদেশ সরকারি কর্মকমিশন। ২৯ কোটি টাকার বিপরীতে সোয়া দুই কোটি টাকা খরচ হয়েছে। সংস্থাটি মোট বরাদ্দের প্রায় সাড়ে ৭ শতাংশ অর্থ ব্যয় করেছে। প্রায় ৭ শতাংশ ব্যয় করেছে সংসদ বিষয়ক সচিবালয়। সাড়ে ৫ শতাংশ অর্থ ব্যয় করেছে মন্ত্রিপরিষদ বিভাগ।

বরাদ্দের ৫ শতাংশ ব্যয় করেছি প্রাথমিক ও গণশিক্ষা মন্ত্রণালয়। সাড়ে ৪ শতাংশ অর্থ ব্যয় করেছে দুর্নীতি দমন কমিশন।

item.description: ত্রয়োদশ জাতীয় সংসদে বিভিন্ন মন্ত্রণালয় ও বিভাগের সংসদীয় কার্যাবলি সম্পাদনের জন্য মন্ত্রীদের দায়িত্ব বণ্টন করেছে সরকার। গতকাল মন্ত্রিপরিষদ বিভাগ থেকে এ-সংক্রান্ত একটি প্রজ্ঞাপন জারি করা হয়েছে।

item.title: Repatriation deadlock pushes Dhaka to rethink Rohingya policy
item.description:
Nine years after the mass Rohingya exodus into Bangladesh, hopes of returning home have faded into deepening uncertainty, with repatriation stalled, violence continuing in Myanmar’s Rakhine State and a worsening humanitarian crisis pushing growing numbers of refugees towards dangerous sea journeys.
More than 1.2 million Rohingya are now living in 32 camps in Ukhiya and Teknaf, nine years after hundreds of thousands fled Myanmar following the military crackdown that began on August 25, 2017.
The population has continued to grow, with 154,690 new arrivals registered between December 2024 and July this year.
For many refugees, the overriding wish remains unchanged: to return safely and with dignity to their homes in Rakhine.
But fighting between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army, which now controls much of Rakhine, has made prospects for repatriation even more remote.
The prolonged uncertainty is increasingly taking a human toll.
UN data cited by Save the Children shows the number of Rohingya attempting to flee Bangladesh and Myanmar by boat has risen 90% from last year.
At least 530 Rohingya who left for Malaysia in July aboard a smugglers’ vessel have remained missing for nearly three weeks.
The trend follows the deadliest year on record for Rohingya sea crossings.
Nearly 900 died or went missing in the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal in 2025, while more than 6,500 attempted the journey.
More than 2,800 had already taken to the sea between January and April 13 this year.
Bangladesh and Myanmar first signed a repatriation agreement in November 2017, followed by arrangements intended to complete returns within two years.
Yet not a single large-scale voluntary repatriation has materialised.
Attempts in 2018 and 2019 collapsed as refugees refused to return without guarantees over citizenship and security.
Myanmar says it has now verified 426,545 of the 828,824 names submitted by Bangladesh, identifying 388,797 as former residents of Rakhine. But verification has produced no timetable for their return.
The diplomatic dispute has meanwhile sharpened.
Myanmar recently rejected accounts of more than one million Rohingya being displaced into Bangladesh and again referred to them as “Bengalis”.
Dhaka formally rejected the terminology and disputed Myanmar’s statistics.
With bilateral repatriation effectively stalled, Bangladesh is increasingly seeking a broader political solution involving Asean, China, Turkey, Malaysia, Norway and other international partners, while pushing for guarantees of citizenship, security and dignified return.
UNHCR spokesperson Shari Yasmin Nijman said conditions inside Myanmar remain unsuitable for voluntary, safe and sustainable repatriation.
“Ultimately, the solution to this crisis lies with Myanmar,” she said, stressing that any return must be voluntary, informed, safe and dignified.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaid Islam echoed that position, saying refugee camps could never become a permanent substitute for a homeland.
“The Rohingya crisis originated in Myanmar, and its sustainable solution must ultimately be found in Myanmar,” she said, calling safe, voluntary and dignified return “the only sustainable path”.
Former ambassador M Humayun Kabir said there was no way to predict how much longer the crisis would continue.
“It will depend on political will,” he said. “If there is political will, it is possible in a shorter time.”
Nine years after the exodus, that political will remains elusive.
For more than a million Rohingya living in Bangladesh, the question is no longer how many repatriation agreements are signed or names verified, but whether any of them will finally open a road home.
